logs.title: Interstellar Travel?
logs.body:
Fortunately, the note app on this tablet is local. They won't see it.

Maybe writing something down will pass what is left of my time.

It looks like we have entered the planet's gravity well. I can feel the pod descending... well, strictly speaking, it is the acceleration and the hull rubbing against the atmosphere.

The fall, a slight deceleration, then something like punching through the planet's brittle surface, followed by a violent shaking... Good thing I am strapped in, though I keep thinking the harness might strangle me.

They have already briefed me on the situation down there—though it cost a string of lives to get that briefing.

...

...Let me think about how to stay alive a little longer...

1. Water, food. There is plenty of stuff they dumped down here with the garbage. Water is not a big problem either, but boiling it first is probably best.

2. Ammo, medical supplies, light. You will not die without them, but you will not get far either.

3. Scavenge some containers and tools. You can live without them, but they will be useful.

That is about it. The roar of the retro thrusters is making it hard to write.

...

Just mixing wolf and human genes would have been hard enough. Add the fact that I do not have cancer or an autoimmune disease, and it looks like they put a lot of work into this "A-version" of me. The data they want is not cheap either.
logs.note: A bioluminescent plant with leaves and stems as brittle as glass, compared to the green plants I know from Earth. The stem glows faintly; the fruit glows. The fruit contains a luminous oxidase, a strong acid, an organic solvent, and a film-forming protective substance. The extract can be used to work metal, plastic, and wood. Do not let it touch skin.
logs.noteLater: I think about the days in the lab, when they tested me through tempered glass with robotic arms. Not pleasant, but... I do not want to die here.

logs.title: STEM-Fish
logs.body:
I remember one test when the robotic arm suddenly stopped. The whole underground facility filled with alarms I had never heard before, along with the shouting, screaming, and gunfire of the other experiments.

The researchers left the lab behind the tempered glass in a hurry. A few security guards in body armor and riot helmets rushed past in the corridor behind them, carrying shotguns.

After a while came a burst of gunfire, shouting, and screaming, then it gradually thinned out.

In the end, only the sound of hard rubber soles on the floor and the blurred, static-laced voices from radios were left in the corridor.

Then the researchers came back—even through the reflective glass, I could feel the change in their expressions.

No one ever talked to me about it afterward, but even a hair (do I have "hair"?) could figure out what happened.

The guards at the door no longer carried only pistols, and new automatic turrets were faintly visible behind the two airlock gates.

...

Now I know. Maybe developing me did cost more than the budget allowed, but the moment the gene sequence was complete, there was no difference between me and the corpses lying among the groundwater pools and the glowing plants.

The same glowing plants in the training sessions were probably clones made from samples brought back by automated probes.

...

But they didn't send a probe on this mission.

Instead...

They sent these SAWs—...

And me.

That points to one answer.

A dedicated probe might be expensive... but experimental subjects—us, the living ones—are inexhaustible.
logs.note: A test robotic arm mounted on the ceiling of the lab. Old, but not rusted; it makes a squeaking mechanical noise when it turns.

logs.title: "Why did they send so many of our kind"
logs.body: This is horrible, this is so fucking horrible, I can't take it anymore, the whole thing is a death pit, there's no hope, it's completely meaningless, why did they send so many of our kind here? It's terrifying, corpses everywhere I look... I'm so scared, why did they send so many of our kind here? I can't figure it out, I really can't figure it out, they knocked me out with something like a dart, stuffed me in a pod and sent me here, I hate this planet.
logs.note:
Written in pencil, pressed hard; the back of the paper is covered in raised strokes. The pencil broke at "I can't figure it out"; the rest is scratched with the broken end, and a few strokes tore through the paper.

It also says "corpses everywhere I look."

I have lost count of how many corpses I passed on the first and second layers. The chip can scan them for me, tagging them as unknown organic matter. Every time, I try to ignore it.

...

Because when I stand in front of the dried blood, fur, meat, and guts, I always feel something I cannot name.

Like... a silence soaking into my brain, forcing me to stand there, ....

In their language, maybe that is a more "vivid" way to put it.

There is another line on the back, erased but still dented: "Will anyone come?"

I... I can only scan this paper and let some tablet's hard drive keep it.

What was his name? I still have not seen any of their names. Only numbers, or nothing at all.

Maybe having a name is, in some sense, the only difference between me and them.

Because I am also down here... never mind. ...

logs.title: Chip Spec // Excerpt
logs.subtitle: Layer 4 · Wasteland · EPDA fragment
logs.body:
...a digital interoceptive device, implanted below the cerebellum and connected to the medulla by conductive nanofilaments. It intercepts visceral and somatic sensory signals, amplifies them, and projects them onto the visual cortex. The unit does not rely on an external battery; it draws power from circulating metabolites and, barring physical damage, can operate indefinitely.

[Maintenance Note 4.2] The unit is sensitive to strong electromagnetic fields. During a solar flare it will enter a degraded mode: timing and positioning functions pause, leaving only basic physiological readings. It recovers on its own after the flare; no manual intervention is required.

[Maintenance Note 4.3] Field maintenance requires a portable signal jammer (standard issue, designation M-114) to take the unit offline first. Any invasive procedure performed while the unit is online is strictly prohibited. Carrier injuries resulting from such a procedure are not classified as equipment failure.

[Work Protocol]
5.1 If the carrier attempts to leave the work area, the unit releases an overload current and terminates carrier activity.
5.2 If the carrier remains on a single layer beyond the time limit, the unit releases high-energy radiation to encourage the carrier to continue descending.
5.3 If the carrier chooses to abandon the mission or refuse to comply, the unit immediately detonates the chip and terminates carrier activity.
5.4 This protocol is not to be disclosed to the carrier.
logs.note:
I pried this EPDA out of the hand of a corpse propped against the rock wall. His fingers had already stiffened; I heard the joints crack as I pulled, like snapping a dry branch. The screen was still on, stopped on the last page he had opened—the same page I would read many times afterward. The wind on the wasteland kept throwing sand at the screen, so I had to turn my back to it and cover it with my coat before I could make out the words.

"Incentive." They printed that word in a clause about killing people, and they printed it formally, as if dying could count as encouragement so long as the wording was restrained enough. I read the passage three times, until my own breath had fogged the screen, before another thought slowly took shape: this document was written for maintenance staff, and if maintenance staff had to touch the unit while it was still running, they had to shut it up first. In other words, they had left themselves a switch. The switch had a name and a number, and it was standard issue—which meant some warehouse had a stack of them, probably more than a few.

I had been in the lab for so long, and no one had ever mentioned it to me. Before every test they just told me to sit still, said it would only take a moment, and then the people behind the glass pointed at a screen. I had always assumed they could touch me whenever they wanted because they were stronger, because they knew more, because they had more right than I did to decide which part of me could be opened. Now I knew: they also had to shut it off first before they dared reach in.

That discovery kept me sitting there for a long time, long enough for the wind to pile sand around my feet. What I thought about then was, frankly, pathetic: if I could get one of those things, at least I might sleep through a night without hearing the chip tell me the depth requirement was not met, without checking my nape every time I turned over to make sure nothing under the skin was heating up.

(The flare silences it. The sky can silence it, and a box can silence it. I cannot carry the sky with me, but if the thing is a box, maybe I can carry it in my pocket.)

logs.title: How Long a Layer Lasts
logs.subtitle: Source: local terminal storage · Layer 5 · Overgrown depths
logs.body:
Layer five has no day or night. The canopy overhead is so thick that even the cold light of the glowing plants cannot get through. I can only count the wounds on my body that have not scabbed over when I wake, and use that to guess how much time has passed. Sleep is not reliable down here. Once I slept too long, and my nape went numb; then a very flat voice in my head said the depth requirement was not met and asked me to speed up, followed by a short burst of static, like someone crushing a glass bead against my ear. I opened my eyes and saw the invisible layer above me pressing down, pressing the spores into a single direction. It took me about two seconds to remember that the chip was feeding signals into my brain, and another two seconds to remember what it would do next.

After that I stopped sleeping through the night. I broke rest into short pieces. Before I closed my eyes I checked my nape for heat; when I woke, the first thing I did was move my fingers to make sure they still obeyed me. When it decides to act, the heat starts at the nape, then the ears, then the fingers. The air on this layer is wet enough to taste; it smells of rotten wood and rust. The water underfoot sometimes reaches my ankles, sometimes my knees. A film of glowing spores floats on the surface; when I walk through it, it scatters, then slowly closes again as if nothing had happened.

I heard the man at the edge of a rock fissure. The sound was not an animal; animals do not breathe in that rhythm, and they do not make a thin, scraping noise between breaths, like fingernails on stone. I lay down and looked through the gap. A man was wedged between two rock walls, head up, one hand stretched outside, fingers still moving. He wore the same kind of protective suit I wore; the number on his chest had been worn away, leaving a pale patch. He was about twelve meters away. I did not go closer, because the gap was too narrow for my shoulders and because by then I could already hear the fine, continuous hum coming from the direction of his nape.

What happened next is very clear to me—so clear that my fingers curl on their own when I write it down. First his nape: the skin began to blacken from the center, slowly, as if someone had lit a lamp under it. Then his ears: the tips curled first, then his cheeks. Then his fingers: one by one they stiffened, and a dark red showed under the nails. He kept moving for much longer than I expected. I do not know why I counted. Maybe it was a habit from training—when something cannot be handled, count. Count to a whole number and the thing will have a result. I counted to forty-three before he stopped.

I sat at the gap for a while before I reached the terminal in and scanned him. The chip's transceiver was still warm. The last three records lay on the screen, small and neatly formatted:

"Depth requirement not met."
"Punishment protocol active."
"Accelerate progress."

The company spoke inside his head until he stopped speaking. What I thought then was that they even killed by procedure: notify first, execute second, and write down the reason in the record afterward. I had seen that system many times in the lab, except the one written into the record back then was not him.
logs.note:
I sat there for thirty minutes and did nothing. The wind went into the gap and moved the corner of his clothes, and more than once I thought he was still breathing.

In the lab, before every test, someone read the procedure aloud: item number, expected minutes, what to do if something went wrong, whether to resuscitate or record first if the carrier lost consciousness. Time was in other people's hands then. I only had to stand—stand while they read, stand while they put the needle in, stand while they said it was over. Now time is still in other people's hands. The only difference is that no one reads it aloud anymore. No one tells me how long is left, and no one tells me how long it will hurt after the limit.

I am not trying to be a hero on layer five. I just do not want to be disposed of at some moment I cannot predict, by a clause I have never read. That was when the jammer became a real thought instead of a word in a file: if the thing exists, if it can really take the chip offline the way the document says, then I have to get one before I reach the end. Otherwise nothing I do matters. I cannot even switch off the thing inside my own body. What else is there to talk about?

(Get it first. As for what to do after that, I had not figured it out yet, and I did not want to.)

logs.title: The One Who Climbed
logs.subtitle: Source: local terminal storage · Layer 6 · Frozen chasm
logs.body:
Layer six is ice. It has not melted in years; the wind has polished it until it shines. It makes a brittle sound underfoot, like stepping on a thin bone. Wind pours down from the top of the cliff, carrying fine ice grains that sting the face like needles. Every so often I have to stop and scrape the frost off my goggles, or the world ahead turns into a single sheet of white.

I saw the marks on a cliff face. At first I thought they were claw marks, because most of the things on this layer have claws and leave deep, long grooves. Up close I saw that the grooves were shallow, one after another, spaced exactly the width of a hand. Some of them still had broken nails in them. Blood was frozen along the edges, dark enough to tell me it had been warm when it was left.

I followed the marks upward for about forty meters and found him under a rock overhang. He hung between two sheets of ice, one hand still hooked into the seam above, the bones pushing through the skin, his face turned upward. His eyes were open; frost had gathered on his lashes. His lips had drawn back, showing his teeth, as if he were smiling. There were no torn wounds on him, no bite marks, no signs of being dragged. He had climbed until he had no strength left, and then he had frozen there.

I went through his pockets and found an empty water bag, half a box of damp matches, and a blade worn down to half its width. His nape was clean—no burn marks from an overload, no black spots seeping through the skin from radiation. I crouched there for a long time before I understood what it meant: going up does not concern the chip. What concerns it is going down, staying too long on one layer, trying to leave the work area. A man going up is walking into the company's hands. Why would the chip care?

That night I propped a small piece of iron on the ice and used it as a mirror to look at my nape. The thing sat slightly to the left; under the skin there was a small, uneven lump that gave a dull ache when pressed. I opened the first cut along its edge with the tip of my knife and barely felt it—the cold had numbed the pain. The second cut had just reached deeper when my nape suddenly burned. A smell of scorched meat rose from inside me, as if someone had pressed a red-hot wire against my spine. My vision narrowed from both sides into a thin slit. I heard myself cry out, the sound very far away, as if it came from the other side of the cliff. Then I found that I was already on my knees on the ice, the knife lying beside me.

I did not try a second time. It does not even need to know what I am thinking. It only needs to know that I moved the knife, and then give me a warning painful enough that I put the knife down myself.
logs.note:
I sat beside the dead man for a long time. He climbed up; I am going down. We both walked obediently along our own roads, and in the end he hangs in the ice and I still have to keep going.

I thought about why he went up. Maybe, like me, he had one day decided he did not want to go down anymore. Maybe he just wanted to see what was above. Maybe he was not thinking at all, and simply found standing better than lying down. I do not know, and I cannot ask. All he left me was half a box of matches and a worn-down blade, not even a number I could read a name from.

The knife does not work. I reached that conclusion on my knees on the ice, and it was clearer than any document: as long as the thing is running, I cannot touch it. Touch it and it will make me stop first. So to cut it out, I have to shut it up first; to shut it up, I have to find the jammer. This layer does not have one. The next layer might not. The one after that might not either. But I have to keep going down. Going down is the only way to have a chance.

I thought about taking the blade. In the end I did not. A blade is for when I can actually use it. Carrying it in my pocket now would only make me feel, at every step, that I could try again—and then make me kneel in the same place again. I put the blade back in his pocket and tucked his outstretched hand into his sleeve, though I knew it made no difference.

logs.title: A Pale Hand's Writing
logs.subtitle: Source: Layer 7 · Fungal pools · In a sandstone crevice
logs.body:
The species distribution here is extremely unbalanced. Experiments are everywhere, far more numerous than individuals like us; in three days I have seen only two still standing. I do not like the casualty figures here. The size is not the problem; the problem is that they have grown so large that no one counts them anymore.

I kept a record: in the same area, eleven Experiments passed in three days, two of them alive. The sample is too small to prove anything, but the trend is not hard to see.

They probably do not know they are part of the numerator.

[Below, in a different hand, smaller and more cramped, as if added later]

Addendum: I may be part of the numerator too. My sample size is just too small to show a trend.
logs.note:
I read it twice, then a third time. The person who wrote this was counting corpses, and counting them neatly: three days, eleven, two alive. He turned his own kind into samples and death into a ratio. The handwriting was small and tidy, every stroke pressed firmly. I know that way of writing. In training I wrote the same way: target area contains three non-active individuals, no threat, recommend advancing. After writing that sentence, my hand did not shake, because the thing on the paper was far away—far enough to be a line of data.

The difference is that after I finished, I would close the notebook and find somewhere quiet to throw up, then come back and finish the rest. He probably did not even bother to throw up, or there was no one around to see him do it.

I walked twenty more steps into the crevice and found him. He sat under a rock, back against the wall, notebook open on his knees, head down, as if asleep. There was pale fur on the back of his hand; his knuckles were thin, his nails neatly trimmed. I touched his wrist. He had been cold for a long time. On the cover of the notebook was a number, soaked by water until only the last two digits were legible. The last page held a single line scratched all the way down; the pen had punched a small hole through the paper.

I turned back through the notebook. On the third page from the end was a line written larger and harder than the rest:

"During the flare, no one on this layer was timed. The chip was dead. When it is dead, a person belongs to himself."

I sat beside him for a long time. Wind came through the crevice and lifted the edge of the notebook again and again; I reached out to hold it down and found that my hand was shaking too. So the lock was not a single piece of iron after all. It had a keyhole, and they had written the shape of the key in their own documents: a flare is a natural jammer; the artificial one is numbered M-114, standard issue, and there is a warehouse full of them. A thing like that would not stay in a warehouse. It would leak out with supplies, stay on the dead, and flow down through the goods the traders carry.

I have to find one. That thought only became "must" instead of "might be useful" after I sat beside a man who turned death into a ratio—and who was still calculating when he died.

logs.title: Dune's Sentences
logs.subtitle: Source: Layer 8 · Crystalline hollow · Under a rock
logs.body:
Planet good. Eat much good meat. Dune happy.

Dune see evil creature. Orange evil creature. Want eat Dune! But Dune fight back, kill and eat evil creature! Creature very tasty!

DUNE find new friend. Friend bite off DUNE arm. DUNE bite off friend arm. Friend go away.

DUNE find him again.

Dune cold. Dig hole not warm enough. Dune eat furry friend. Eat raw! Dune have fur, fur warm. Dune full and warm.

Dune love tasting friends. Dark fur tough, light fur chewy.

What Dune taste like?
logs.note:
I read it three times before I was sure it was not madness. It has no grammar and the punctuation is a mess, but every sentence is true: it really ate those things, it really wrote "friend bit off DUNE's arm" and "DUNE bit off friend's arm" as two equal events, and it was probably licking its fingers while it wrote. There is only one question mark in the whole thing, at the end.

I was trained. I can tell how many exits a room has in two seconds, estimate how many days a corpse has been dead from the stiffness, and hear in the dark whether the footsteps belong to a person or something else. It can do none of that. It does not even have the word "tomorrow." It knows cold, hunger, pain, and warmth. And yet the question it asked at the end is the one I have been asking myself for days. I ask what the point is. It asks what it tastes like. I cannot answer. If I had to, I would say salty. All the water, all the meat, all the wounds down here are salty.

It was probably measured too—skull circumference, blood draws, a form with a column called "expected survival," filled in with a number of days. It does not know that. Right now it only wants to be warm.

I folded the paper and put it away, then went deeper into the cave and came across the pod.

A trader sat inside, built on the same skeleton as me, with pale fur and a dorsal fin. The light from the pod wall made half his face very white. He had not come down here; he sold things here. When I walked up, he raised his head and asked what I needed in a practiced voice—the same voice as the sales talk I had heard in the lab, only slower, flatter, like a recording.

I did not answer at once. I put my hand on the pod glass and looked at his face for a while. He looked back. After a moment he put his own hand against mine, palm to palm, with the glass between us. Then he asked what I needed.

I asked whether he had anything that could shut a chip up. He did not answer immediately. After a while he reached into the pod and brought out an unremarkable grey box, then pushed it toward me. A small line was stamped on the bottom: M-114. Below it, another line: single use, valid for one layer's key only.

I asked how much. He named a price so low that I hesitated—probably because he did not know what was in the box, or because he did know, and to a man who sells things from a pod it was no different from a roll of bandages. I counted out what I had and gave it to him. He pushed the box over and then stopped looking at me, as if the sale had never happened.

I asked how to use it. He took a long time to answer, and when he did it was the same sales voice, in the same tone as the price. I asked three times before he added one sentence: save it. You only get one.

(He is cleaner than I am. I could tell from the hand he pressed against the glass: nails whole, fur even, not a single scar. He has never been down a shaft, and he has never pressed a hand over someone else's wound at the bottom of one.)

I put the box in my pocket and walked a long way before I stopped. Single use, one layer only. I did not know which layer to use it on, but I knew it had to be the lowest one. The cargo is there, the route starts closing there, and after that layer everything I do will be written into their records. So I cannot waste it before then, and I cannot let anyone know I have it.

logs.title: Cargo Spec // Wireless Power Unit
logs.subtitle: Source: Layer 9 · Geothermal vents · Abandoned container
logs.body:
...can store an enormous amount of electrical energy and distribute it wirelessly to nearby equipment; equivalent output far exceeds any existing solution of the same volume. The casing is single-piece, seamless, and cannot be disassembled. The internal structure cannot be reproduced with current manufacturing.

[Incident] Teleport calibration error. The unit did not land on the surface; it entered the deep cave system. Incident class: A. Responsible party: pending.

[Disposition] Dispatch a carrier to descend and search. The search route is recorded by the chip; the carrier must not leave the work area.

[Assessment]
Search success rate: low
Carrier survival rate: not assessed
Consumable materials: sufficient
Assessment result does not affect execution

[Note] If the casing is damaged, do not touch it with bare hands. Confirm carrier status before recovery. Carrier status is not a recovery condition.

[Attachment] The unit may be used as a power source for high-power equipment within its rated output; test records are attached. This is not the purpose of recovery.
logs.note:
Carrier status is not a recovery condition. I read that sentence several times, until each word felt very light, as if someone else were saying it. The grammar is clean: the box is cargo, I am the carrier; if the carrier breaks, replace it, but the cargo must not break. Below it is an even cleaner line: consumable materials are sufficient, and the assessment result does not affect execution. In other words, before they sent anyone down, they had already calculated that the person sent would most likely not come back, and that calculation did not make anyone stop and reconsider.

I turned the page. On the back was a flow chart. It began with descent and had four arrows: descend, search, carry, return. The last arrow stepped over my body and landed in a box labeled "disposal." I stared at that box for a long time, until the heat from the vents curled the edge of the paper, and then the pieces of the journey finally came together: they made me so that I could get here; they let me get here so that I could bring the thing back; and as for what happens after I bring it back, the chart is quite clear, though it does not specify the method.

(If the box could walk, they would not have needed to make me. They made me because the box cannot walk, and a walking cargo handler costs less than a machine that can reach this depth.)

I noticed something else: the thing is a wireless power unit, with an output so absurdly high that it can run high-power equipment within its rated range. The document put that in an attachment and took care to add "this is not the purpose of recovery," as if afraid someone would think they had come down here to power something. For me, that attachment was more useful than the main text. It meant that once the thing was inside me, I would not be just a bag holding cargo; I would be a bag holding a power source. If anything up there needed electricity, I would have a reason to stand there until they explained themselves.

What if I do not hand it over? The first time that thought appeared, it startled me, because until then I had been thinking only about how to stay alive, how to take one less dose of radiation, how to wake up before the next time I fell asleep. But now I read the flow chart again and again, and I saw that the only part of the route left unexplained was what happens after I hand it over; the only part I could decide for myself was whether I would still be willing to hand it over when the time came.

I did the timing. The unit is on layer ten. Once I have it, there is only one route left: back to the pod, return, deliver. Every step is recorded. Every step has someone waiting. If I am going to move, it has to be on layer ten, at the moment I take it, or before. The jammer works on one layer only, and that layer is layer ten. It works once, and that once is then.

I took the box out of my pocket and looked at it in my palm. It was very light, too light to decide anything.

logs.title: It Came to Me
logs.subtitle: Source: local terminal storage · Layer 10 · WHERE WE MUST REACH
logs.body:
Layer ten has no forks. One main road runs straight from the landing point, rock walls burned by something on both sides, and at the end of it is a pod. The hatch is open. The lights inside are dark. A thin layer of dust covers the console.

Three people sit at the pod door. Two lean together; one lies face down. All three are dried out. The air here is so dry that the bodies did not rot; they only shrank, skin stuck to bone like old paper. They have no cargo on them, and none beside them. Their packs are empty, their water bags are empty, even their magazines are empty. I walked around inside the pod. A line is carved into the console in very small letters: THIS POD REQUIRES AN EXTERNAL HIGH-POWER SOURCE. The letters are cut deep, as if someone traced them with the tip of a knife, one stroke at a time, and then perhaps sat down to wait.

(So they made it here. They could not leave. The last few dozen meters, and they sat down with their own exit.)

Behind the pod is a fissure leading down. It is not wide—just enough for a person to squeeze through sideways. There is light below, blue, pulsing, like a heartbeat. As I climbed down, I could feel the light brighten with my movement; the crystals in the rock bent it back and made my fingers look as if they were underwater.

The thing clings to the rock at the bottom of the fissure. It is the size of a palm, blue, shaped like a heart. It pulses, and the light brightens and dims with the pulse; when it dims, I can see a fine network of lines on its surface, like veins. When I was three steps away, it stopped.

Then it came toward me, clinging to the rock, first sliding slowly out of place, then faster and faster, until all I could see was a blue streak.

I did not move. Why I did not move, I cannot say—perhaps because the fissure was too narrow, perhaps because I had come down for it, perhaps because in that instant it occurred to me that being approached by something on its own was better than being arranged by a document. When it struck my abdomen, I felt cold first; the cold was quickly covered by heat, and then by a pain that is hard to describe, a pain that opened me from the inside. I looked down and saw my clothes pushed up in one place, something moving under the skin, as if a hand had reached into my belly, found a place, and sat down.

I heard myself cry out. The sound was very far away, as if it came from the other end of the fissure. I held on to the rock, my nails digging into the crystal seams, and the pain lasted about two minutes. Then it receded like a tide, leaving only a hot, hard object against the inside of my abdominal wall, rising and falling with my heartbeat.

Then I became lighter, as if someone had peeled an invisible layer off my body.

When I raised my arm, it moved faster than I remembered. When I stood, my knees did not creak. Every battery bar on the terminal was full; even the flashlight was brighter than usual. I touched my abdomen. There was a hard place there; pressing it hurt, but the pain was strange—as if my body had already accepted it and was only reminding me not to push too hard.

(They put a power station in my belly and still expect me to be grateful.)

I climbed back up the fissure into the pod. The console lights came on, and a line of text slowly surfaced on the screen: MSN-CARGO / RETURN--BASE. The hatch was open, and the lights inside were on now, warm, completely different from the blue light outside.

Above me is layer eleven. Above that is the surface. Above that is their laboratory.

variants.note:
[Layer 10]

I opened my nape when I entered this layer. When the jammer was pressed against the skin, the area went numb, then lost all feeling. The knife went in more easily than I expected; blood ran down my neck and into my collar, hot, as if someone else had poured it there. When I pulled the thing out, it was still glowing, a thin filament connecting it to something deeper; I had to pull twice before it broke. When it broke, I heard something click inside my head, and then there was silence.

I had never experienced that kind of silence. There used to be something in my nape, like a machine running in a room you have grown used to; you stop hearing it. Now the machine had stopped, and only then did I learn how empty the room could be.

It crawled into my abdomen while I was awake. It still hurt, but this time it was only pain. Nothing in my head was recording how long it lasted, how bad it was, or whether it needed to be reported. I knelt on the ground, holding the rock, and waited for it to pass. When it passed, I stood up and found that I walked more steadily than I had on the way down.

(They put a power station in my belly and still expect me to be grateful. The power station is mine now. We can talk about gratitude later.)

The pod should start now. Above is layer eleven, then the surface, then their laboratory.

I will go up, the cargo is in me, and I am not handing it over.

[Layer 10]

I did not cut it out, and the jammer is still in my pocket, cold as a piece of ordinary iron. I sat at the entrance to this layer for a long time, took it out and put it back, took it out again, and in the end did nothing. I gave myself a reason: cutting it might leave me unable to finish the descent; brain damage would make me a burden in the last layers. The real reason is that I was afraid—afraid that when the knife went in, it would act first; afraid that I would die in a slit I had opened myself; afraid of the pain. Write it down. No one is likely to read this.

It crawled into my abdomen while I was awake. It still hurt, and the thing in my nape was still there, counting quietly. For a moment I even felt it watching, watching another thing crawl into the body it had managed for so many years, and recording that too.

The pain lasted about two minutes. Then I became lighter; my arm moved faster than I remembered; every battery bar on the terminal was full. I touched my abdomen. The hard thing lay against my abdominal wall, rising and falling with my heartbeat.

(They put a power station in my belly and still expect me to be grateful.)

Above is layer eleven, then the surface. They can still press the button, but they cannot make a second one of these. As long as it is inside me, they will have to think before they press it.

[Layer 10]

I never got the thing. I saw M-114 only once, in the note on that document. Later I asked at several traders; some did not understand, some shook their heads, some went through everything in the pod and came out with nothing. Maybe I could not afford it. Maybe I asked the wrong way. Maybe things like that never flow downward at all—they stay in the lab, for people in white coats.

The thing in my nape is still counting. It has been steady, not once missing a beat since I came down.

It crawled into my abdomen while I was awake. It still hurt, and the thing in my nape was still there. While I hurt, it was probably recording too—my heart rate, my blood pressure, how long the pain lasted, how this carrier performed while loading cargo.

The pain lasted about two minutes. Then I became lighter; my arm moved faster than I remembered; every battery bar was full.

Now I am complete: a walking carrier, cargo loaded, route fixed. They are probably satisfied.

(I am not. I write that down because writing it down is all I can do.)

logs.title: On Signatures
logs.subtitle: Source: local terminal storage · CRIMSON ASCENT
logs.body:
Layer eleven is called the Crimson Ascent. The name is accurate: the steps are red, rising one after another, with no end in sight. At first I thought it was iron rust in the rock. Halfway up I saw that the red was something seeping out, drying and wetting again, wetting and drying again, until it had laid a thin layer over the stone. In some places the marks run downward, which means the people who bled there were standing, or crawling, but not lying down.

I climb with the cargo. Every step makes the thing in my belly send out another pulse of heat, as if it were counting the steps for me. By the end I do not need to look to know how many are left, because the heat comes faster and hotter.

Halfway up, I stop and go through everything I have scanned on the way down.

The things I have seen line up in my head one by one: the man whose timer ran out, the hand frozen in the ice, the recorder who sat down on a rock and died, the three at the pod door who ran out of power. None of them was an accident. Every one of them died on a neatly written document: consumable materials sufficient, carrier survival rate not assessed, terminate carrier activity, disposal. The people who wrote those words are in the laboratory now, waiting for me to bring the cargo up.

I will bring it up, because if I do not, I will never reach a room with people in it.

I go through the documents again, looking for whoever wrote them. Not one of them has a signature—only departments, titles, numbers. Even the copy that came down with my pod is the same: the paper is new, the printing is clean, and the signature line still holds only a title. At first I thought it was the damp. Then I understood: they never intended to leave their names on it.

An institution that does not need signatures is very convenient. The document carries only a title; who sits behind the title does not matter. Put someone else in the chair and the same signature comes out. That way no one has to be responsible for a document, and no one has to lie awake at night thinking about a number. They did it so cleanly that even the dead I passed on the way down are only rows in a table, without a name left behind.

I write in the first person; they write me in the third. It is the same person, but in their version I am never "he." From beginning to end I am "the carrier." Carrier status is not a recovery condition. If the carrier arrives on its own, the on-site supervisor will handle it. If the carrier is incapacitated, the site will clean up. I read those sentences aloud, to the steps, to the thing in my belly, and when I finished I felt as if I had been reading someone else's eulogy.

(Why do they not leave their own names? I think it is because a name means responsibility, and no one wants to be responsible for what they do. So they erase the names, neatly, with a standard format. A thing that will not even leave its own name has no right to ask me to remember a number. I remember my number, SF-07. I remember it clearly, because apart from that number they never gave me anything.)

...

When I reach the top of the steps, the sky is grey, the clouds pressed low, as if they might fall at any moment. Something comes down out of the clouds: round, four legs, almost silent when it lands. It stops a short distance ahead of me, hatch open, the light inside warm. I have seen many life-support pods, but this one is different—it lands too precisely, as if it knew exactly where I would come up.

It is here to collect me. I can tell from where it landed.

I stand still. Wind comes through the open hatch, carrying a clean smell that makes me uncomfortable. I know the procedure: board, sleep, return to the lab, unload, and then I enter the disposal process. I also know that if I turn around and walk back, they will write "carrier refused return" in the record, then press the button, or send something else down.

I do not turn around. The thing in my belly has begun to stir in the sunlight. First a faint tremble, then a twist, then another, as if someone were turning over inside my abdominal wall. Every minute it twists harder, until the pain makes me bend over. I suddenly understand why they are not afraid I will refuse the pod: they do not need to send anyone to catch me. The thing will drive me in by itself.

So I will go up, even if going up means walking into the room they have prepared for me.

At the lab, they will not tackle me at the pod door. They will talk to me first, make me believe I can survive, make me walk through the door myself. That is how they have done it all the way down—clauses, time limits, the promise of "just one more layer," step by step, until I stand where they want me. So before I walk through that door, there is a very short gap. Short enough for only a few sentences, but I get to choose which ones. I will demand to see the signer. I will demand that he stand in front of me and read the words "carrier incapacitated" out loud.

(If he does not come, I will keep the cargo inside me, for as long as I can. They cannot make a second one; I cannot last long, but they cannot gamble on how long I have left.)

variants.note:
[Written at the end]

The cut on my nape has scabbed over. It still hurts when the wind blows, but the pain is clean, and when it passes there is nothing left. No voice, no counting, no one in my head telling me the depth requirement is not met. This is the first time I have come up to the surface with a quiet nape.

They cannot press the button anymore. The first thing I have ever owned is worth more than the cargo.

I will board the pod as they ask, because the cargo will not last long in sunlight. But boarding is not the same as following their procedure. At the lab, I will stop at the door of that operating room and demand to see the signer. I will demand that he read "carrier incapacitated" to my face. After he reads it, I will decide whether to lie down on the table.

(This terminal's drive will probably say only "carrier incapacitated, data not recovered." If you are reading this, I am already gone, and these words are still here. Then they are all I have left. —SF-07)

[Written at the end]

The jammer is still on layer ten. Outside that layer it is a piece of plastic; I tried it, and nothing happened. The thing in my nape is still counting, probably in hours.

I am still going up, because the cargo is in my belly and it will start making trouble after a few minutes in the sun. They probably counted on that. They counted on me walking into the pod myself. But they missed one thing: they say carrier status is not a recovery condition, yet the document also says to confirm carrier status before recovery. They do not want to kill me at the door. A living carrier is easier to handle than a corpse, and no one needs to teach me that.

So I will stop at the operating room door and demand to see the signer. I will demand that he read "carrier incapacitated" to my face. If they refuse, I will stand there. If they move against me, I will make sure they understand that breaking me and the cargo together will cost them far more than letting me speak.

(They will probably write it all up as a malfunction. I would rather call it a fight back, even if this is the only one I get. —SF-07)

[Written at the end]

I never even touched the jammer. M-114 appeared only in the note on that document, and I never saw a second one. The thing in my nape is still counting; it has not missed a beat since I came down.

I am still going up, because the cargo is in my belly and it will start making trouble after a few minutes in the sun. I have no key to the chip and no other bargaining chip, only the thing in my belly that they cannot make again. They probably think I am finished: a carrier, cargo loaded, route fixed, and all I have to do is walk into the pod and the whole job is done.

I will walk into the pod. But I will stop at the operating room door and demand to see the signer. I will demand that he read "carrier incapacitated" to my face. My life stopped being mine the day they put the chip in; now at least it can buy a few sentences. I will use those sentences to make them say what they did, and say it to themselves.

(They will probably call it a necessary loss. Then I will make them say the word "necessary" to my face again. —SF-07)
